opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I felt pretty uncertain. The summer internship had been a great experience. I learned a lot about how real research works, how you go from a vague idea to experiments to something you can actually write up. But when I came back to Tsinghua and started putting the applications together, I had to look at my profile honestly, and it wasn't as strong as I'd hoped.

I didn't have a first-author paper at a top venue. The work from the summer was promising, but it wasn't finished in a way I could point to and say, "This is my result." A lot of my classmates were applying to the same top PhD programs, and many of them had really impressive records. So I knew it would be competitive, and I couldn't count on getting into the places I wanted most.

At the same time, I felt I'd grown a lot. I had a clearer sense of what I liked, which was reinforcement learning, and of building systems that actually work rather than only chasing benchmark numbers. I also had my open-source projects, which I thought showed something about how I work, even if they don't fit neatly into a traditional application. So my mindset was to apply broadly, write as honestly as I could about what I'd done and what I wanted to do, and be prepared for different outcomes. If the PhD route didn't work out, a master's or going straight into industry wouldn't be the end of the world. Keeping that in mind actually made the whole process a lot less stressful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Jiayi lacked a first-author paper and expected competition, but does not say applicants without one were generally screened out.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was pretty anxious. When I got back to Tsinghua that fall, the summer internship had gone well, but it also showed me how big the gap was between me and the people I'd be competing against. I'd spent the summer working alongside students who already had papers at top venues, who had advisors with real name recognition, and I came back with a project that wasn't finished and a recommendation letter I wasn't sure would carry much weight.

So I remember sitting down with my list of schools and thinking, realistically, which of these would even read my application seriously? My GPA was fine, not spectacular. My research experience was real but thin. I didn't have a first-author paper yet. And I was applying for PhD programs in a field where everyone and their cousin suddenly wanted to do machine learning. That year the application numbers were exploding.

What helped me was that I stopped thinking about it as "will I get in somewhere prestigious" and started thinking about it as "what can I actually control in the next three months." I could polish the project into something presentable. I could write a statement that was honest about what I'd done and clear about what I wanted to do next. I could reach out to a couple of professors whose work I genuinely cared about, not just the famous ones. And I could keep contributing to the open-source stuff I'd been doing on the side, because that was the one thing I had that most applicants didn't.

So my prospects, as I saw them then, were a coin flip at best for the schools I really wanted, and decent for the safety options. I think I was more realistic than optimistic. But looking back, the anxiety actually made me do better work, because I knew I couldn't coast on credentials I didn't have.

r001.rationale: The candidate says she had no first-author paper and wondered whether schools would take her application seriously, but does not convey a belief that applicants without one were generally screened out.
